analysis.one_liner: Requires offshore oil drilling to use the best available blowout preventers and emergency shutoff equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, this bill would have directed the Interior Department to write rules requiring every offshore oil and gas operation to have safety systems in place, including blowout preventers and backup emergency shutoff equipment like acoustic shut-off technology, using the best available technology. It would have applied to new operations immediately and existing ones six months after the rules were issued, and required a technology review every five years. The bill was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, Gulf fishermen, tourism businesses, and offshore workers would gain if the bill passed, because better shutoff equipment reduces the chance of a catastrophic spill that devastates fisheries, beaches, and local economies. Taxpayers would also avoid some of the cleanup and liability costs spills create.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fishermen, and tourism workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires all offshore drilling and production operations to have safety and environmental management systems, including blowout preventers and additional backup emergency shutoff equipment such as acoustic shut-off technology.

Requires that the equipment use the best available and safest technologies, with regulations written within six months of enactment and applied to new operations immediately and existing operations six months later.

Requires the Interior Department to review blowout preventer and shutoff technology every five years and update the rules as needed, and directs the Energy Department to identify the best available and safest offshore technology.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies drilling offshore would bear the cost of installing and maintaining the required backup safety equipment, and some of those costs could be passed on in energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Requiring additional backup emergency shutoff equipment on every offshore operation imposes upfront equipment and compliance costs on drilling companies, costs that could be passed to consumers through higher prices.
Requiring the Interior Department to issue rules within six months of enactment is a tight deadline that could produce rushed rulemaking and litigation over the standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow, well-understood failure mode: the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster showed blowout preventers can fail, and acoustic shutoff backup is a modest, targeted fix. The compliance cost to drillers is real but small compared with the multi-billion-dollar damage a single deepwater blowout causes to fisheries, coastlines, and local economies. The six-month rulemaking deadline is aggressive but not a reason the bill failed; it simply never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two committees and then to subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2011 by Rep. Jay Inslee with bipartisan cosponsors and referred to the Natural Resources and Energy and Commerce Committees.
On April 19 and April 25, 2011 it was referred to the Energy and Mineral Resources and Energy and Power subcommittees respectively.
No further action was taken, and the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress without a committee or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas drillers benefited because they never faced the new equipment mandates, and coastal communities and the public gained no added protection from the safety rules the bill would have required.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drillers; coastal protections never materialized

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start, with a Democratic sponsor and four cosponsors split evenly between two Republicans and two Democrats, so opposition came from inaction rather than a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas drilling companies
industries.note: Drillers would have had to install and maintain additional backup emergency shutoff equipment and use best available technology, raising their operating costs. Better equipment protects the public and coastal economies from the cost of catastrophic spills.
These businesses bear enormous losses when a blowout fouls fisheries and beaches, as the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill showed. Stronger shutoff requirements directly reduce that risk.
